differential_diagnoses.name: Chronic pancreatitis
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Diffuse parenchymal calcifications and ductal dilation on CT, without a discrete mass; CA 19-9 typically normal or only mildly elevated.

differential_diagnoses.name: Autoimmune pancreatitis
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Diffuse 'sausage-shaped' pancreatic enlargement with a capsule-like rim and elevated serum IgG4; responds rapidly to corticosteroids.

differential_diagnoses.name: Cholangiocarcinoma
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Dominant biliary stricture with a normal pancreatic parenchyma; CA 19-9 may be elevated but imaging shows a hilar or distal bile duct mass rather than a pancreatic head mass.

differential_diagnoses.name: Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Hypervascular mass on contrast-enhanced imaging with early arterial enhancement, often associated with hormonal syndromes; chromogranin A may be elevated.

differential_diagnoses.name: Metastasis to the pancreas
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Multiple pancreatic lesions in a patient with a known primary (e.g., renal cell carcinoma, melanoma); history and immunohistochemistry of a biopsy specimen confirm the primary site.

key_features: Painless jaundice with a palpable gallbladder (Courvoisier sign) in tumors of the pancreatic head.
Weight loss, anorexia, and new-onset diabetes mellitus in a patient over 50 years.
Contrast-enhanced CT showing a hypoenhancing pancreatic mass with upstream ductal dilation (double-duct sign).
Elevated CA 19-9, often >100 U/mL, though it can be normal in Lewis-negative individuals.
Endoscopic ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration confirming adenocarcinoma.
pitfalls: Often mistaken for chronic pancreatitis because both cause weight loss, abdominal pain, and pancreatic atrophy; a discrete mass and progressive ductal dilation favor malignancy.
The underlying diagnosis is missed when new-onset diabetes or unexplained weight loss is attributed to aging or metabolic syndrome without imaging.

differential_diagnoses.name: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Incremental response on repetitive nerve stimulation (facilitation >200%) and antibodies to voltage-gated calcium channels; proximal leg weakness and autonomic symptoms are prominent.

differential_diagnoses.name: Botulism
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Acute descending symmetric paralysis with fixed dilated pupils and no response to edrophonium; history of contaminated food or wound exposure.

differential_diagnoses.name: Miller Fisher syndrome
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, and areflexia with anti-GQ1b antibodies; acute onset after infection and absent fatigable weakness.

differential_diagnoses.name: Thyroid eye disease
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Proptosis, lid retraction, and restrictive ophthalmoplegia with abnormal thyroid function tests; no fatigable ptosis or limb weakness.

differential_diagnoses.name: Congenital myasthenic syndromes
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Onset in infancy, family history, and absence of acetylcholine receptor antibodies; genetic testing confirms the diagnosis.

key_features: Fatigable weakness that worsens with activity and improves with rest, typically affecting ocular, bulbar, and proximal limb muscles.
Ptosis and diplopia as the most common presenting symptoms.
Positive acetylcholine receptor antibodies in ~85% of generalized cases; anti-MuSK antibodies in a subset.
Decrement >10% on repetitive nerve stimulation at 2–3 Hz.
Thymoma or thymic hyperplasia on chest imaging; thymectomy may improve symptoms.
pitfalls: Often mistaken for a stroke or anxiety when presenting with diplopia or dysarthria because symptoms fluctuate and examination may be normal between episodes.
The diagnosis is missed when isolated ocular symptoms are attributed to age-related ptosis or dry eye without testing for fatigability.

differential_diagnoses.name: Primary CNS lymphoma
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Contrast-enhancing mass lesion with restricted diffusion and often periventricular location; biopsy shows monoclonal B cells, and CSF may show elevated IL-10.

differential_diagnoses.name: Toxoplasma encephalitis
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Multiple ring-enhancing lesions with surrounding edema, typically in basal ganglia; responds to pyrimethamine-sulfadiazine, and serology for Toxoplasma is positive.

differential_diagnoses.name: Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis (ADEM)
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Monophasic illness with multifocal white matter lesions that enhance with gadolinium and follow a viral illness; CSF may show pleocytosis, and lesions are not typically progressive.

differential_diagnoses.name: CNS vasculitis
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Vessel wall thickening and enhancement on high-resolution MRI, with angiographic beading; brain biopsy shows transmural inflammation, not viral inclusions.

differential_diagnoses.name: HIV encephalopathy
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Diffuse symmetric white matter hyperintensities without mass effect or enhancement, and CSF HIV RNA is elevated; no JC virus DNA in CSF.

key_features: Subacute progressive focal neurological deficits (hemiparesis, aphasia, visual field cuts) in an immunocompromised patient (e.g., HIV/AIDS, natalizumab therapy).
MRI showing asymmetric, non-enhancing white matter lesions without mass effect, often involving subcortical U-fibers.
Detection of JC virus DNA in CSF by PCR.
Brain biopsy showing demyelination with enlarged oligodendrocytes containing viral inclusions and bizarre astrocytes.
CD4 count <200 cells/µL or use of immunosuppressive monoclonal antibodies.
pitfalls: Often mistaken for a stroke because of acute focal deficits, but the progression over weeks and MRI pattern of non-enhancing white matter lesions should prompt JC virus testing.
The underlying immunosuppression is overlooked when PML is the first presentation of HIV; HIV testing should be routine.

differential_diagnoses.name: Meconium plug syndrome
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Passage of a meconium plug after rectal stimulation or enema, with normal ganglion cells on biopsy; typically resolves without surgery.

differential_diagnoses.name: Intestinal pseudo-obstruction
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Recurrent episodes of obstruction with normal ganglion cells and absence of the rectoanal inhibitory reflex; may be secondary to systemic disease.

differential_diagnoses.name: Cystic fibrosis
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Meconium ileus with a microcolon and family history; sweat chloride test is diagnostic, and ganglion cells are present.

differential_diagnoses.name: Hypothyroidism
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Constipation and poor feeding with elevated TSH and low free T4; resolves with thyroid hormone replacement.

differential_diagnoses.name: Anal stenosis
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Narrow anal canal on physical examination with normal ganglion cells; responds to dilation.

key_features: Delayed passage of meconium beyond 48 hours of life in a term infant.
Abdominal distension and bilious vomiting in the neonatal period.
Barium enema showing a transition zone with a narrow aganglionic segment and dilated proximal colon.
Absence of the rectoanal inhibitory reflex on anorectal manometry.
Rectal biopsy showing absence of ganglion cells and hypertrophied nerve trunks.
pitfalls: Often mistaken for functional constipation in older children because of chronic constipation, but the absence of the rectoanal inhibitory reflex and a transition zone on enema should prompt biopsy.
The diagnosis is missed when meconium plug syndrome is treated with enemas without considering Hirschsprung disease, especially if symptoms persist.

differential_diagnoses.name: Burkitt lymphoma
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Medium-sized cells with a 'starry sky' pattern and a Ki-67 proliferation index near 100%; MYC translocation is characteristic.

differential_diagnoses.name: Follicular lymphoma
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Nodular architecture with centrocytes and centroblasts, and t(14;18) translocation; typically indolent and CD10+.

differential_diagnoses.name: Hodgkin lymphoma
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Reed-Sternberg cells in an inflammatory background, CD15+ and CD30+, with absent CD20; usually nodal and contiguous spread.

differential_diagnoses.name: Mantle cell lymphoma
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Small to medium cells with cyclin D1 overexpression and t(11;14); typically CD5+ and CD23−.

differential_diagnoses.name: Metastatic carcinoma
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Carcinoma cells are cytokeratin-positive and CD45-negative; clinical history and immunohistochemistry distinguish from lymphoma.

key_features: Rapidly enlarging painless lymph node or extranodal mass (e.g., gastrointestinal, testicular, CNS).
B symptoms: fever, night sweats, and weight loss.
Biopsy showing diffuse sheets of large lymphoid cells with a high mitotic rate and CD20+ B-cell phenotype.
Elevated lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) and beta-2 microglobulin.
PET-CT showing hypermetabolic uptake in involved sites.
pitfalls: Often mistaken for an infection or reactive lymphadenopathy because of fever and lymphadenopathy; lack of response to antibiotics and progressive enlargement should prompt biopsy.
The diagnosis is missed when extranodal presentations (e.g., testicular mass, bone lesion) are attributed to other causes without tissue sampling.

differential_diagnoses.name: Acute tubular necrosis
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Muddy brown casts and a fractional excretion of sodium >2% in the setting of ischemia or nephrotoxins; no eosinophiluria or sterile pyuria.

differential_diagnoses.name: Glomerulonephritis
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Active urinary sediment with dysmorphic red blood cells and red cell casts, and proteinuria often >1 g/day; biopsy shows glomerular inflammation.

differential_diagnoses.name: Pyelonephritis
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Fever, flank pain, and positive urine culture with leukocyte esterase; responds to antibiotics, and imaging may show focal changes.

differential_diagnoses.name: Renal atheroembolic disease
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Eosinophilia, livedo reticularis, and recent vascular catheterization; biopsy shows cholesterol clefts in arterioles.

key_features: Acute kidney injury developing days to weeks after starting a culprit drug (e.g., NSAIDs, antibiotics, proton pump inhibitors).
Sterile pyuria with white blood cell casts and mild proteinuria.
Eosinophiluria and peripheral eosinophilia (though nonspecific).
Renal biopsy showing interstitial edema and lymphocytic infiltrate with eosinophils.
Improvement after withdrawal of the offending agent; corticosteroids may hasten recovery.
pitfalls: Often mistaken for acute tubular necrosis because both cause acute kidney injury in hospitalized patients; the presence of sterile pyuria, eosinophiluria, and a temporal drug relationship favor AIN.
The underlying drug cause is missed when multiple medications are started simultaneously; a thorough medication timeline is essential.

differential_diagnoses.name: Medial meniscal tear
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Joint line tenderness and a positive McMurray test; MRI shows a meniscal tear, whereas pes anserine bursitis has tenderness 2–3 cm distal to the joint line.

differential_diagnoses.name: Medial collateral ligament sprain
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Tenderness along the MCL with valgus stress pain; no focal swelling over the pes anserine bursa.

differential_diagnoses.name: Osteoarthritis of the knee
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Crepitus, reduced range of motion, and radiographic joint space narrowing; bursitis pain is localized below the joint line.

differential_diagnoses.name: Popliteal cyst
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Posterior knee swelling and ultrasound showing a fluid-filled cyst in the popliteal fossa; not tender at the medial proximal tibia.

key_features: Focal tenderness over the pes anserine bursa, located 2–3 cm distal to the medial joint line of the knee.
Pain worsened by climbing stairs, rising from a chair, or direct pressure.
Localized swelling or fullness at the medial proximal tibia.
Ultrasound showing fluid distension of the bursa.
Often associated with obesity, diabetes, or knee osteoarthritis.
pitfalls: Often mistaken for a medial meniscal tear because of medial knee pain; the location of tenderness below the joint line and absence of mechanical symptoms distinguish it.
The diagnosis is missed when pain is attributed to osteoarthritis without palpating the pes anserine bursa.

differential_diagnoses.name: Vasovagal syncope
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Prodrome of warmth, nausea, and diaphoresis, often triggered by prolonged standing or emotional stress; situational syncope occurs during or immediately after a specific activity (e.g., micturition, defecation, cough).

differential_diagnoses.name: Orthostatic hypotension
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Drop in systolic blood pressure ≥20 mmHg or diastolic ≥10 mmHg within 3 minutes of standing; symptoms occur on standing, not during a specific activity.

differential_diagnoses.name: Cardiac arrhythmia
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Syncope without prodrome, often during exertion or supine; ECG monitoring shows arrhythmia, and there is no situational trigger.

differential_diagnoses.name: Seizure
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Postictal confusion, tonic-clonic movements, and lateral tongue biting; EEG shows epileptiform activity, and there is no situational trigger.

key_features: Syncope occurring during or immediately after micturition, defecation, coughing, or swallowing.
Prodromal symptoms such as lightheadedness, diaphoresis, or nausea may be present.
Rapid recovery without postictal confusion.
Blood pressure and heart rate may show transient bradycardia or hypotension during the event.
Diagnosis is clinical, based on a clear temporal relationship with the trigger.
pitfalls: Often mistaken for a seizure because of brief loss of consciousness, but the situational trigger and lack of postictal state distinguish it.
The diagnosis is missed when syncope is attributed to a cardiac cause without eliciting a history of situational triggers.

differential_diagnoses.name: Congenital cytomegalovirus infection
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Periventricular calcifications and sensorineural hearing loss; urine CMV PCR is positive, and rubella IgM is negative.

differential_diagnoses.name: Congenital toxoplasmosis
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Diffuse intracranial calcifications and hydrocephalus; Toxoplasma IgM/IgA are positive, and rubella serology is negative.

differential_diagnoses.name: Congenital syphilis
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Snuffles, bone lesions (osteochondritis), and positive treponemal tests; rubella serology is negative.

differential_diagnoses.name: Congenital Zika syndrome
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Severe microcephaly with cortical malformations and ocular abnormalities; Zika IgM is positive in serum or CSF, and rubella serology is negative.

key_features: Sensorineural hearing loss, often bilateral and severe.
Cataracts, congenital heart disease (e.g., patent ductus arteriosus, pulmonary artery stenosis), and microcephaly.
Blueberry muffin rash (extramedullary hematopoiesis) at birth.
Positive rubella IgM in the newborn or persistent IgG beyond 6 months of age.
History of maternal rubella infection during the first trimester.
pitfalls: Often mistaken for other congenital infections (CMV, toxoplasmosis) because of overlapping features; specific serology is required for differentiation.
The diagnosis is missed when mild hearing loss or a single anomaly is attributed to other causes without considering maternal rubella history.

differential_diagnoses.name: Fibroadenoma
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Small, mobile, well-circumscribed mass with uniform stromal and epithelial proliferation; phyllodes tumors typically grow rapidly and have leaf-like architecture with stromal hypercellularity.

differential_diagnoses.name: Breast carcinoma
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Irregular, firm mass with skin changes or nipple retraction; biopsy shows malignant epithelial cells, not a biphasic stromal-epithelial proliferation.

differential_diagnoses.name: Juvenile hypertrophy
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Diffuse bilateral breast enlargement in adolescents without a discrete mass; phyllodes tumor is a distinct mass.

differential_diagnoses.name: Metaplastic carcinoma
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Carcinoma with sarcomatoid differentiation; immunohistochemistry shows cytokeratin positivity in the malignant cells, whereas phyllodes tumor has a benign epithelial component.

key_features: Rapidly growing, painless breast mass, often large (>3 cm).
Imaging showing a well-circumscribed, lobulated mass with cystic spaces.
Core biopsy showing a biphasic tumor with leaf-like fronds and stromal hypercellularity.
Stromal atypia and mitoses distinguish borderline and malignant phyllodes tumors.
Most common in women aged 40–50 years.
pitfalls: Often mistaken for a fibroadenoma because both are well-circumscribed masses; rapid growth and large size should raise suspicion for phyllodes tumor.
The diagnosis is missed when a rapidly growing mass is assumed to be a benign fibroadenoma without excision or biopsy.

differential_diagnoses.name: Pelvic inflammatory disease
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Cervical motion tenderness and adnexal tenderness, often with salpingitis; endometritis alone may have uterine tenderness without adnexal involvement.

differential_diagnoses.name: Endometrial cancer
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Postmenopausal bleeding with endometrial thickening on ultrasound; biopsy shows malignant cells, not inflammation.

differential_diagnoses.name: Ectopic pregnancy
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Positive pregnancy test and adnexal mass; endometritis is not associated with pregnancy unless postpartum.

differential_diagnoses.name: Vaginitis
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Vaginal discharge and itching without uterine tenderness; wet mount shows the causative organism.

key_features: Fever, lower abdominal pain, and abnormal uterine bleeding.
Uterine tenderness on bimanual examination.
Purulent cervical discharge or foul-smelling lochia in postpartum cases.
Endometrial biopsy showing neutrophils in the endometrial mucosa.
Risk factors: recent delivery, miscarriage, or uterine instrumentation.
pitfalls: Often mistaken for pelvic inflammatory disease because of overlapping symptoms; endometritis is confined to the uterus, while PID involves the adnexa.
The diagnosis is missed when postpartum fever is attributed to mastitis or urinary tract infection without pelvic examination.

differential_diagnoses.name: Anal fissure
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Sharp, tearing pain with defecation and a visible linear tear in the anal canal; hemorrhoids typically cause painless bleeding unless thrombosed.

differential_diagnoses.name: Colorectal cancer
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Rectal bleeding with altered bowel habits, weight loss, and iron deficiency anemia; colonoscopy shows a mass, not engorged vascular cushions.

differential_diagnoses.name: Perianal abscess
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Severe throbbing pain, fever, and a fluctuant perianal mass; hemorrhoids are not fluctuant or associated with systemic signs.

differential_diagnoses.name: Rectal prolapse
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Full-thickness protrusion of the rectal wall with concentric folds; hemorrhoids show radial folds and are covered by mucosa.

key_features: Painless bright red blood per rectum, typically coating the stool or on toilet paper.
Prolapsing tissue during defecation that may reduce spontaneously or require manual reduction.
Perianal itching or discomfort.
Visible engorged vascular cushions on anoscopy.
Symptoms worsened by constipation, prolonged sitting, or pregnancy.
pitfalls: Often mistaken for colorectal cancer because of rectal bleeding; age >50, weight loss, or anemia should prompt colonoscopy.
The diagnosis is missed when bleeding is attributed to hemorrhoids without digital rectal examination or anoscopy.

differential_diagnoses.name: Absence seizure
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Brief (5–10 s) staring spells with 3-Hz spike-and-wave on EEG and no postictal confusion; complex partial seizures last longer and have automatisms and postictal confusion.

differential_diagnoses.name: Transient ischemic attack
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Sudden focal neurological deficit without impaired awareness or automatisms; symptoms are typically negative (e.g., weakness) and resolve within 24 hours.

differential_diagnoses.name: Psychogenic nonepileptic seizure
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Prolonged duration, asynchronous movements, and closed eyes; EEG shows no epileptiform activity during the event.

differential_diagnoses.name: Migraine with aura
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Visual or sensory aura followed by headache; no impaired consciousness or automatisms, and EEG is normal.

key_features: Impaired awareness with staring, lip smacking, or hand automatisms.
Aura (e.g., déjà vu, unusual smell, epigastric rising sensation) preceding the event.
Postictal confusion and fatigue.
EEG showing focal temporal or frontal epileptiform discharges.
MRI may show a structural lesion (e.g., hippocampal sclerosis, tumor).
pitfalls: Often mistaken for a psychiatric disorder because of behavioral automatisms and impaired awareness; EEG and witness history are key.
The diagnosis is missed when brief episodes of confusion are attributed to transient ischemic attacks without considering seizure semiology.

differential_diagnoses.name: Anterior hip dislocation
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Leg held in external rotation and abduction; posterior dislocation presents with internal rotation and adduction.

differential_diagnoses.name: Femoral neck fracture
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Shortened, externally rotated leg without fixed flexion; radiograph shows a fracture line, not dislocation.

differential_diagnoses.name: Hip fracture-dislocation
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Concomitant acetabular or femoral head fracture on CT; pure dislocation has no fracture.

differential_diagnoses.name: Sciatic nerve injury
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Foot drop and sensory loss in the sciatic distribution; may accompany posterior dislocation but is not the primary diagnosis.

key_features: Severe hip pain after high-energy trauma (e.g., dashboard injury).
Leg held in flexion, adduction, and internal rotation.
Inability to bear weight.
Radiograph showing the femoral head displaced posteriorly and superiorly relative to the acetabulum.
Associated sciatic nerve palsy in 10–20% of cases.
pitfalls: Often mistaken for a hip fracture because of severe pain and inability to walk; the characteristic leg posture and radiograph distinguish dislocation.
The diagnosis is missed when sciatic nerve palsy is attributed to a primary nerve injury without recognizing the dislocation.

differential_diagnoses.name: Mallet finger
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Inability to extend the distal interphalangeal joint, with a flexed posture; jersey finger affects flexion at the DIP joint.

differential_diagnoses.name: Volar plate injury
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Pain and swelling at the volar proximal interphalangeal joint with hyperextension injury; DIP flexion is preserved.

differential_diagnoses.name: Trigger finger
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Clicking or locking during flexion with a palpable nodule at the A1 pulley; no acute trauma and active DIP flexion is intact.

differential_diagnoses.name: Flexor tendon laceration
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Laceration over the volar finger with inability to flex the DIP joint; history of sharp injury rather than avulsion.

key_features: Inability to actively flex the distal interphalangeal joint after a forced extension injury (e.g., grabbing a jersey).
Tenderness and swelling over the volar distal phalanx.
The affected finger rests in extension at the DIP joint.
Radiograph may show a bony avulsion fragment at the volar base of the distal phalanx.
Most commonly affects the ring finger.
pitfalls: Often mistaken for a sprain because swelling is mild and pain may be tolerable; testing active DIP flexion is essential.
The diagnosis is missed when a bony avulsion is overlooked on radiographs and the injury is treated as a simple contusion.

differential_diagnoses.name: Pilar cyst (trichilemmal cyst)
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Pilar cysts are typically on the scalp, firm, and lack a central punctum; histology shows abrupt keratinization without a granular layer, unlike epidermoid cysts which have a granular layer and a central punctum.

differential_diagnoses.name: Lipoma
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Lipomas are soft, doughy, and mobile; ultrasound shows a hyperechoic mass, whereas epidermoid cysts are firm and ultrasound shows a well-defined hypoechoic mass with posterior enhancement and no vascularity.

differential_diagnoses.name: Dermoid cyst
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Dermoid cysts are congenital, often midline or periorbital, and may contain hair, teeth, or sebaceous glands on imaging; epidermoid cysts are acquired and typically lack these elements.

differential_diagnoses.name: Abscess
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Abscess presents with acute inflammation, pain, and fluctuance; ultrasound shows a complex fluid collection with irregular walls and surrounding hyperemia, while epidermoid cysts are well-circumscribed and avascular.

key_features: Firm, dome-shaped nodule with a central punctum (comedo) and possible cheesy malodorous discharge.
Commonly found on the face, neck, trunk, or scrotum.
Ultrasound: well-defined, round, hypoechoic mass with posterior acoustic enhancement and no internal vascularity.
Histology: cyst lined by stratified squamous epithelium with a granular layer and lamellated keratin.
May become inflamed or infected, mimicking an abscess.
pitfalls: Often mistaken for a sebaceous cyst, but epidermoid cysts are not true sebaceous cysts and lack sebaceous glands in the wall.
Rupture can cause a foreign-body inflammatory reaction that is misdiagnosed as an infection, leading to unnecessary antibiotics.

differential_diagnoses.name: Ulcerative colitis
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Ulcerative colitis typically presents with bloody diarrhea and chronic symptoms; C. difficile colitis is acute, often after antibiotic use, and stool testing for C. difficile toxin or PCR is positive.

differential_diagnoses.name: Ischemic colitis
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Ischemic colitis usually affects the watershed areas (splenic flexure) and presents with pain out of proportion and hematochezia; C. difficile colitis often involves the entire colon and is associated with antibiotic exposure and positive stool testing.

differential_diagnoses.name: Infectious diarrhea (e.g., Salmonella, Shigella)
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Other infections may have positive stool cultures for pathogens; C. difficile is diagnosed by toxin detection or PCR, and pseudomembranes on endoscopy are characteristic.

differential_diagnoses.name: Antibiotic-associated diarrhea without colitis
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Antibiotic-associated diarrhea is usually mild and self-limited without systemic signs; C. difficile colitis presents with fever, leukocytosis, abdominal pain, and positive stool testing.

key_features: History of recent antibiotic use (e.g., clindamycin, fluoroquinolones, cephalosporins).
Watery diarrhea, abdominal pain, fever, and leukocytosis.
Stool testing positive for C. difficile toxin A/B or PCR.
Endoscopy may show pseudomembranes (yellowish plaques).
Complications include toxic megacolon, perforation, and sepsis.
pitfalls: Often misdiagnosed as nonspecific antibiotic-associated diarrhea when mild, leading to delayed testing and treatment.
The diagnosis can be missed in patients without recent antibiotic exposure (community-acquired) or in those with atypical presentations such as ileus.

differential_diagnoses.name: Infectious ulcer (e.g., bacterial, fungal)
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Infectious ulcers have positive wound cultures and respond to antimicrobials; pyoderma gangrenosum is sterile and diagnosed by exclusion, with negative cultures.

differential_diagnoses.name: Venous stasis ulcer
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Venous ulcers are typically painless or mildly painful, located near the medial malleolus, with surrounding edema and hemosiderin staining; pyoderma gangrenosum is painful, has a violaceous undermined border, and often occurs on the legs but without venous insufficiency signs.

differential_diagnoses.name: Sweet syndrome
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Sweet syndrome presents with tender erythematous plaques and neutrophilic infiltrate without ulceration; pyoderma gangrenosum has ulcers with undermined borders and a different histologic pattern (neutrophilic dermal infiltrate with ulceration).

differential_diagnoses.name: Squamous cell carcinoma
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Squamous cell carcinoma is a malignant ulcer with rolled edges and atypical keratinocytes on biopsy; pyoderma gangrenosum is a neutrophilic dermatosis with negative malignancy on biopsy.

key_features: Painful, rapidly enlarging ulcer with a violaceous, undermined border and purulent base.
Commonly associated with inflammatory bowel disease, rheumatoid arthritis, and hematologic malignancies.
Pathergy: worsening after trauma or surgery.
Diagnosis of exclusion: negative cultures and no evidence of infection or malignancy.
Histology: dense neutrophilic infiltrate with ulceration and necrosis.
pitfalls: Often misdiagnosed as an infection, leading to unnecessary debridement and antibiotics, which can worsen the condition due to pathergy.
Underlying systemic disease (e.g., IBD, malignancy) is missed when the skin lesion is not recognized as a marker.

differential_diagnoses.name: Placental abruption
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Abruption presents with painful vaginal bleeding, uterine tenderness, and fetal distress; uterine rupture often has sudden severe pain, loss of fetal station, and fetal bradycardia, with bleeding that may be intraperitoneal rather than vaginal.

differential_diagnoses.name: Uterine dehiscence
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Dehiscence is an incomplete rupture with intact serosa and often asymptomatic; rupture involves full-thickness tear with fetal extrusion and acute symptoms.

differential_diagnoses.name: Chorioamnionitis
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Chorioamnionitis presents with fever, uterine tenderness, and foul amniotic fluid; uterine rupture is characterized by sudden pain, fetal distress, and loss of station, often without fever.

differential_diagnoses.name: Ovarian torsion
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Ovarian torsion causes sudden unilateral pelvic pain with nausea and vomiting, but fetal heart tracing is usually normal; uterine rupture shows fetal heart rate abnormalities and may have vaginal bleeding.

key_features: Sudden severe abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding, and fetal heart rate abnormalities (bradycardia, late decelerations).
Loss of fetal station and cessation of contractions.
History of prior cesarean section or uterine surgery.
Maternal tachycardia, hypotension, and shock.
Ultrasound may show fetal parts outside the uterus or free fluid.
pitfalls: Often mistaken for placental abruption or normal labor pain, delaying diagnosis and increasing maternal/fetal morbidity.
The classic signs (loss of station, fetal distress) may be absent in early or incomplete rupture, leading to underestimation.

differential_diagnoses.name: Lumbar spinal stenosis
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Spinal stenosis causes neurogenic claudication (pain with walking, relieved by sitting) and is often bilateral; disc herniation typically causes unilateral radicular pain in a dermatomal pattern, worsened by sitting and Valsalva.

differential_diagnoses.name: Piriformis syndrome
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Piriformis syndrome causes buttock pain and sciatica-like symptoms, but MRI shows no disc herniation; tenderness over the piriformis and positive Freiberg test help differentiate.

differential_diagnoses.name: Facet joint arthropathy
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Facet arthropathy causes axial back pain worsened by extension and rotation, without radicular symptoms; disc herniation typically causes radicular pain with positive straight leg raise.

differential_diagnoses.name: Spinal epidural abscess
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Epidural abscess presents with fever, severe back pain, and neurologic deficits; MRI shows an epidural collection, whereas disc herniation shows disc material compressing the nerve root.

key_features: Radicular pain in a dermatomal distribution (e.g., L5 or S1).
Positive straight leg raise test (Lasègue sign).
Motor, sensory, or reflex deficits corresponding to the affected nerve root.
MRI showing disc material protruding beyond the annulus fibrosus.
Pain worsened by sitting, coughing, or sneezing.
pitfalls: Often misdiagnosed as nonspecific low back pain when radicular symptoms are not elicited, leading to delayed imaging.
Caution: cauda equina syndrome (saddle anesthesia, bowel/bladder dysfunction) can be missed if not specifically asked about.

differential_diagnoses.name: Toxoplasmic retinochoroiditis
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Toxoplasmosis typically presents as a focal necrotizing retinochoroiditis with a pigmented scar and vitritis; CMV retinitis has a “pizza-pie” or “brushfire” appearance with hemorrhage and minimal vitritis.

differential_diagnoses.name: Acute retinal necrosis (ARN)
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: ARN (due to HSV/VZV) shows rapid peripheral necrosis with prominent vitritis and vasculitis; CMV retinitis is usually indolent, with granular necrosis and hemorrhage, often perivascular.

differential_diagnoses.name: HIV retinopathy
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: HIV retinopathy presents with cotton-wool spots and microaneurysms without necrosis or hemorrhage; CMV retinitis has dense necrotic areas with hemorrhage and is vision-threatening.

differential_diagnoses.name: Syphilitic retinitis
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Syphilitic retinitis often has a “salt-and-pepper” fundus and positive syphilis serology; CMV retinitis is diagnosed by characteristic funduscopic appearance and positive CMV PCR in aqueous humor.

key_features: Painless, progressive vision loss in an immunocompromised patient (e.g., advanced HIV with CD4 <50 cells/µL).
Funduscopy: yellow-white granular necrosis with hemorrhage, often in a “pizza-pie” or “brushfire” pattern.
Minimal vitritis (“quiet” vitreous).
Positive CMV PCR in aqueous or vitreous humor.
Risk of retinal detachment.
pitfalls: Often mistaken for HIV retinopathy (cotton-wool spots) leading to delayed treatment and vision loss.
The diagnosis can be missed in patients with atypical presentations or when the fundus is not adequately visualized.

differential_diagnoses.name: Septic arthritis
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Septic arthritis presents with acute monoarthritis, fever, and positive synovial fluid culture; reactive arthritis is sterile, often oligoarticular, and follows a recent infection (e.g., Chlamydia, Salmonella).

differential_diagnoses.name: Psoriatic arthritis
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Psoriatic arthritis is associated with psoriasis and nail changes, and is seronegative; reactive arthritis typically has a preceding infection and classic triad of arthritis, urethritis, and conjunctivitis.

differential_diagnoses.name: Gout
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Gout presents with acute monoarthritis (often first MTP), hyperuricemia, and negatively birefringent crystals in synovial fluid; reactive arthritis is oligoarticular and lacks crystals.

differential_diagnoses.name: Ankylosing spondylitis
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Ankylosing spondylitis is chronic, starts in the sacroiliac joints, and is associated with HLA-B27; reactive arthritis is acute, often self-limited, and follows an infection.

key_features: Oligoarthritis (often knees, ankles) following a recent gastrointestinal or genitourinary infection.
Classic triad: arthritis, urethritis, and conjunctivitis (Reiter syndrome).
HLA-B27 positivity in many cases.
Sterile synovial fluid with elevated white blood cell count.
May have enthesitis (e.g., Achilles tendinitis) or mucocutaneous lesions (keratoderma blennorrhagicum, circinate balanitis).
pitfalls: Often misdiagnosed as septic arthritis due to acute joint inflammation, leading to unnecessary antibiotics and joint drainage.
The preceding infection may be asymptomatic and not reported, so the diagnosis is missed.

differential_diagnoses.name: Seborrheic keratosis
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Seborrheic keratosis has a “stuck-on” appearance, comedo-like openings, and no atypical melanocytes on biopsy; melanoma shows asymmetry, border irregularity, and atypical melanocytes.

differential_diagnoses.name: Basal cell carcinoma
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Basal cell carcinoma often has a pearly border with telangiectasias and ulceration; melanoma is usually pigmented with irregular borders and may show a blue-white veil on dermoscopy.

differential_diagnoses.name: Dysplastic nevus
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Dysplastic nevus may share features with melanoma but lacks severe atypia, mitoses, and pagetoid spread on histology; melanoma shows malignant features and may have BRAF mutations.

differential_diagnoses.name: Pigmented squamous cell carcinoma
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Pigmented SCC may have keratin pearls and no melanocytic markers; melanoma is positive for S100, HMB-45, and Melan-A.

key_features: Asymmetric, irregularly bordered, multi-colored lesion (ABCDE criteria).
Dermoscopy: atypical network, blue-white veil, irregular dots/globules.
Histology: atypical melanocytes with pagetoid spread, mitoses, and Breslow thickness.
Positive immunohistochemistry for S100, HMB-45, Melan-A.
Risk factors: UV exposure, fair skin, family history, multiple nevi.
pitfalls: Often mistaken for a benign nevus or seborrheic keratosis, leading to delayed biopsy and diagnosis.
Amelanotic melanoma can be misdiagnosed as a benign inflammatory lesion or basal cell carcinoma.

differential_diagnoses.name: Celiac disease
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Celiac disease is diagnosed by positive tissue transglutaminase IgA and duodenal biopsy showing villous atrophy; IBS has no such biomarkers and symptoms are functional.

differential_diagnoses.name: Inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn's/UC)
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: IBD shows elevated fecal calprotectin, inflammatory markers, and endoscopic/histologic inflammation; IBS has normal biomarkers and no visible inflammation.

differential_diagnoses.name: Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO)
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: SIBO is diagnosed by positive lactulose or glucose breath test; IBS is a diagnosis of exclusion based on Rome criteria.

differential_diagnoses.name: Colorectal cancer
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Colorectal cancer may present with alarm features (rectal bleeding, weight loss, anemia) and is detected by colonoscopy; IBS lacks alarm features and has normal colonoscopy.

key_features: Recurrent abdominal pain at least 1 day per week in the last 3 months, associated with defecation or change in stool frequency/form (Rome IV).
Symptoms chronic (≥6 months) and not explained by other conditions.
Subtypes: IBS-D (diarrhea), IBS-C (constipation), IBS-M (mixed).
Normal physical exam, lab tests, and colonoscopy (if indicated).
Symptoms often exacerbated by stress and certain foods.
pitfalls: Often misdiagnosed as IBD or celiac disease due to overlapping symptoms, leading to unnecessary testing and delayed reassurance.
Alarm features (e.g., weight loss, rectal bleeding) may be overlooked, missing a serious organic disease.

differential_diagnoses.name: Ovarian cancer with ascites
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Ovarian cancer typically has complex solid/cystic masses, elevated CA-125, and malignant cells on cytology; Meigs syndrome has a benign fibroma, resolves after resection, and ascites is reactive.

differential_diagnoses.name: Tuberculous peritonitis
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Tuberculous peritonitis presents with ascites, fever, and positive TB culture/PCR; Meigs syndrome has a pelvic mass and no infection.

differential_diagnoses.name: Cirrhotic ascites
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Cirrhotic ascites is associated with liver disease, portal hypertension, and low serum-ascites albumin gradient; Meigs syndrome has a pelvic mass and normal liver function.

differential_diagnoses.name: Nephrotic syndrome
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Nephrotic syndrome causes ascites due to hypoalbuminemia and proteinuria; Meigs syndrome has a pelvic mass and no significant proteinuria.

key_features: Benign ovarian fibroma (or other benign ovarian tumor) with ascites and pleural effusion.
Ascites and pleural effusion resolve after tumor resection.
CA-125 may be elevated but normalizes postoperatively.
No malignant cells in ascitic fluid.
Often presents with abdominal distension and shortness of breath.
pitfalls: Often misdiagnosed as ovarian cancer with peritoneal carcinomatosis, leading to unnecessary chemotherapy or extensive surgery.
The benign nature of the ovarian mass may be overlooked, and the patient may be treated for cirrhosis or heart failure.

differential_diagnoses.name: Primary biliary cholangitis
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: PBC primarily affects small intrahepatic bile ducts, is associated with anti-mitochondrial antibodies (AMA), and shows florid duct lesions; PSC affects large ducts, is AMA-negative, and shows “beaded” strictures on cholangiography.

differential_diagnoses.name: Secondary sclerosing cholangitis
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Secondary causes (e.g., stones, surgery, ischemia) are identified; PSC is idiopathic and associated with IBD (especially ulcerative colitis).

differential_diagnoses.name: Cholangiocarcinoma
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Cholangiocarcinoma presents with a dominant stricture and malignant cells on brush cytology; PSC has multifocal strictures and is a risk factor for cholangiocarcinoma.

differential_diagnoses.name: IgG4-related sclerosing cholangitis
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: IgG4-related disease shows elevated serum IgG4 and abundant IgG4-positive plasma cells on biopsy; PSC lacks these and is associated with IBD.

key_features: Cholestatic liver enzyme pattern (elevated ALP and GGT).
Cholangiography: multifocal strictures and dilatations (“beaded” appearance).
Strong association with inflammatory bowel disease (ulcerative colitis).
p-ANCA positivity in some cases.
Increased risk of cholangiocarcinoma and colorectal cancer.
pitfalls: Often misdiagnosed as primary biliary cholangitis due to cholestatic labs, but AMA is negative and cholangiography is diagnostic.
The association with IBD is missed, and patients are not screened for colorectal cancer.

differential_diagnoses.name: Urinary tract infection
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: UTI has positive urine culture and responds to antibiotics; interstitial cystitis has negative cultures and chronic symptoms.

differential_diagnoses.name: Bladder cancer
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Bladder cancer may present with hematuria and is diagnosed by cystoscopy and biopsy; interstitial cystitis shows Hunner's ulcers or glomerulations but no malignancy.

differential_diagnoses.name: Overactive bladder
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Overactive bladder causes urgency and frequency without pain; interstitial cystitis is characterized by pain with bladder filling and relief after voiding.

differential_diagnoses.name: Endometriosis
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Endometriosis may cause cyclic pelvic pain and is diagnosed by laparoscopy; interstitial cystitis has bladder-specific symptoms and cystoscopic findings.

key_features: Chronic pelvic pain, pressure, or discomfort related to the bladder, with urinary frequency and urgency.
Pain worsened by bladder filling and relieved by voiding.
Negative urine cultures and no other identifiable cause.
Cystoscopy may show Hunner's ulcers or glomerulations after hydrodistension.
Diagnosis of exclusion based on symptoms and cystoscopy.
pitfalls: Often misdiagnosed as recurrent UTI due to frequency and urgency, leading to repeated unnecessary antibiotic courses.
Symptoms may be attributed to overactive bladder, missing the pain component and delaying appropriate therapy.

differential_diagnoses.name: Rotator cuff tear
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Rotator cuff tear presents with weakness and positive impingement signs, and MRI shows tendon tear; adhesive capsulitis has global restriction of motion, especially external rotation, with normal MRI except capsular thickening.

differential_diagnoses.name: Glenohumeral osteoarthritis
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Osteoarthritis shows joint space narrowing, osteophytes, and sclerosis on X-ray; adhesive capsulitis has normal X-ray and global motion loss.

differential_diagnoses.name: Calcific tendinitis
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Calcific tendinitis shows calcific deposits on X-ray and acute severe pain; adhesive capsulitis has gradual onset and no calcifications.

differential_diagnoses.name: Septic arthritis
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Septic arthritis presents with fever, severe pain, and positive synovial fluid culture; adhesive capsulitis is afebrile and chronic.

key_features: Gradual onset of shoulder pain and progressive loss of both active and passive range of motion, especially external rotation.
Three phases: freezing (painful), frozen (stiff), thawing (recovery).
X-rays are normal; MRI may show capsular thickening and rotator interval enhancement.
Associated with diabetes mellitus and thyroid disease.
Diagnosis is clinical.
pitfalls: Often misdiagnosed as rotator cuff tendinitis or impingement, leading to inappropriate exercises that worsen pain.
The significant restriction of passive motion is not tested, missing the diagnosis.

differential_diagnoses.name: SIADH due to other causes (e.g., CNS disorders, drugs)
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Other causes of SIADH are identified by history (e.g., medications, CNS pathology); in lung cancer, imaging shows a pulmonary mass and biopsy confirms malignancy.

differential_diagnoses.name: Adrenal insufficiency
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Adrenal insufficiency presents with hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and hypotension; SIADH has euvolemia, normal potassium, and low serum osmolality with high urine osmolality.

differential_diagnoses.name: Hypothyroidism
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Hypothyroidism causes hyponatremia with elevated TSH and low free T4; SIADH has normal thyroid function tests.

differential_diagnoses.name: Congestive heart failure
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: CHF causes hypervolemic hyponatremia with edema and elevated BNP; SIADH is euvolemic with low BNP.

key_features: Hyponatremia with low serum osmolality and high urine osmolality.
Euvolemia and normal adrenal/thyroid function.
Underlying lung cancer (often small cell lung cancer).
Symptoms of hyponatremia: confusion, seizures, coma.
Imaging shows a lung mass; biopsy confirms cancer.
pitfalls: Often misdiagnosed as SIADH from other causes (e.g., medications) without imaging the chest, missing the underlying lung cancer.
Hyponatremia may be attributed to chemotherapy or other comorbidities, delaying cancer diagnosis.

differential_diagnoses.name: Septic arthritis (nongonococcal)
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Nongonococcal septic arthritis typically involves a single joint with positive synovial fluid culture for organisms like Staphylococcus aureus; DGI often causes tenosynovitis and dermatitis, and synovial fluid cultures are often negative.

differential_diagnoses.name: Reactive arthritis
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Reactive arthritis is sterile and follows an infection, with negative cultures; DGI has positive NAAT for N. gonorrhoeae and responds to antibiotics.

differential_diagnoses.name: Meningococcemia
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Meningococcemia presents with rapidly progressive purpura and shock; DGI has fewer, scattered pustules and tenosynovitis, and positive gonococcal testing.

differential_diagnoses.name: Endocarditis
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Endocarditis may cause embolic phenomena and positive blood cultures; DGI typically has tenosynovitis and dermatitis, and blood cultures are often negative.

key_features: Triad: tenosynovitis, dermatitis (pustules), and polyarthralgias.
Recent genital infection or new sexual partner.
Positive NAAT for Neisseria gonorrhoeae from mucosal sites or joint fluid.
Blood cultures are positive in only ~30% of cases.
Responds rapidly to ceftriaxone.
pitfalls: Often misdiagnosed as reactive arthritis due to joint symptoms, but DGI has positive gonococcal testing and responds to antibiotics.
Skin lesions may be overlooked, and the diagnosis is missed if a sexual history is not obtained.

differential_diagnoses.name: Transient tachypnea of the newborn
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Chest X-ray shows perihilar streaking and fluid in the fissures without low lung volumes or ground-glass opacities; resolves within 24-72 hours.

differential_diagnoses.name: Meconium aspiration syndrome
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Chest X-ray shows patchy infiltrates and hyperinflation, not the uniform ground-glass appearance with low lung volumes of RDS; history of meconium-stained fluid.

differential_diagnoses.name: Neonatal pneumonia
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Chest X-ray shows focal or asymmetric infiltrates and may have positive blood culture; RDS shows symmetric ground-glass opacities with air bronchograms.

differential_diagnoses.name: Congenital diaphragmatic hernia
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Chest X-ray shows bowel loops in the hemithorax and mediastinal shift; RDS shows diffuse ground-glass opacities without bowel loops.

differential_diagnoses.name: Congenital heart disease (e.g., cyanotic lesions)
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Echocardiography reveals structural heart defect; in RDS, echocardiography is normal and hypoxia responds to positive pressure ventilation.

key_features: Tachypnea, grunting, nasal flaring, and retractions within minutes to hours after birth, especially in preterm infants.
Chest X-ray: low lung volumes, diffuse reticulogranular (ground-glass) opacities, and air bronchograms.
Arterial blood gas: hypoxemia and hypercapnia, often requiring supplemental oxygen and positive pressure ventilation.
Deficiency of pulmonary surfactant, confirmed by lecithin/sphingomyelin ratio <2 or absent phosphatidylglycerol in amniotic fluid.
Response to exogenous surfactant administration with rapid improvement in oxygenation and decreased ventilatory requirements.
pitfalls: Often mistaken for transient tachypnea of the newborn because both cause early respiratory distress; TTN is differentiated by chest X-ray showing perihilar streaking and fluid in fissures, and by rapid resolution.

The diagnosis is missed when respiratory distress in a preterm infant is attributed solely to prematurity without considering early-onset sepsis or pneumonia, which may coexist and require antibiotics.

differential_diagnoses.name: Mantle cell lymphoma
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Immunophenotype: CD5+, CD23−, FMC7+, cyclin D1+ (t(11;14)); CLL is CD5+, CD23+, FMC7−, and cyclin D1−.

differential_diagnoses.name: Hairy cell leukemia
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Immunophenotype: CD11c+, CD25+, CD103+, CD123+, and BRAF V600E mutation; CLL is CD5+, CD23+, and lacks these markers.

differential_diagnoses.name: Follicular lymphoma
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Immunophenotype: CD10+, CD5−, BCL2+ with t(14;18); CLL is CD5+, CD23+, and CD10−.

differential_diagnoses.name: Monoclonal B-cell lymphocytosis
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Peripheral blood B-cell count <5 × 10^9/L; CLL requires ≥5 × 10^9/L clonal B cells.

differential_diagnoses.name: Prolymphocytic leukemia
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: >55% prolymphocytes on peripheral smear; CLL has <55% prolymphocytes.

key_features: Persistent lymphocytosis (≥5 × 10^9/L) with mature-appearing small lymphocytes and smudge cells on peripheral smear.
Immunophenotype: CD5+, CD19+, CD23+, CD20 (dim), surface immunoglobulin (dim), and FMC7−.
Lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly; bone marrow infiltration by small lymphocytes.
Hypogammaglobulinemia and increased susceptibility to infections, especially encapsulated bacteria.
Advanced disease may present with cytopenias (anemia, thrombocytopenia) due to marrow replacement or autoimmune destruction.
pitfalls: Often mistaken for reactive lymphocytosis because both show increased lymphocytes; CLL is differentiated by clonality on flow cytometry (kappa/lambda light chain restriction) and CD5/CD23 co-expression.
The diagnosis is missed when smudge cells are dismissed as artifact and flow cytometry is not performed, delaying recognition of the clonal B-cell disorder.

differential_diagnoses.name: Acute decompensation of cirrhosis
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Evidence of chronic liver disease (e.g., cirrhosis on imaging, varices, ascites, low platelets) and often a precipitating event; fulminant hepatic failure occurs in a previously healthy liver without chronic changes.

differential_diagnoses.name: Sepsis-induced liver dysfunction
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Positive blood cultures and hemodynamic instability with improvement of liver tests after sepsis control; fulminant hepatic failure shows massive transaminase elevation and coagulopathy disproportionate to sepsis.

differential_diagnoses.name: Acute fatty liver of pregnancy
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Occurs in the third trimester with microvesicular steatosis, hypoglycemia, and elevated ammonia; resolves with delivery, whereas fulminant hepatic failure has other causes and does not resolve with delivery.

differential_diagnoses.name: Wilson disease (acute presentation)
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Low serum ceruloplasmin, elevated urinary copper, and Kayser-Fleischer rings; fulminant hepatic failure from other causes lacks these copper abnormalities.

differential_diagnoses.name: Autoimmune hepatitis (severe acute)
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Positive antinuclear antibody (ANA) and anti-smooth muscle antibody (ASMA), elevated IgG, and interface hepatitis on biopsy; fulminant hepatic failure of other etiologies lacks these autoantibodies.

key_features: Coagulopathy (INR ≥1.5) and hepatic encephalopathy developing within 26 weeks of onset of illness in a patient without pre-existing cirrhosis.
Massive elevation of aminotransferases (often >1000 U/L) followed by falling transaminases and rising bilirubin as liver function deteriorates.
Jaundice, asterixis, and altered mental status; cerebral edema is a major cause of death.
Multisystem involvement: acute kidney injury, hypoglycemia, lactic acidosis, and susceptibility to infections.
Etiologic workup: acetaminophen levels, viral hepatitis serologies, autoimmune markers, and imaging to exclude vascular causes (e.g., Budd-Chiari).
pitfalls: Often mistaken for acute decompensation of cirrhosis because both present with jaundice and encephalopathy; fulminant hepatic failure is distinguished by the absence of chronic liver disease signs and by massive transaminase elevation.
The underlying cause (e.g., acetaminophen toxicity) is missed when history is unreliable and levels are not obtained, delaying administration of N-acetylcysteine.

differential_diagnoses.name: Aortic stenosis
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Echocardiography shows a stenotic aortic valve with reduced excursion and a systolic ejection murmur at the right upper sternal border; coarctation shows a discrete narrowing in the descending aorta with a systolic pressure gradient between arms and legs.

differential_diagnoses.name: Essential hypertension
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Equal blood pressures in all four limbs and no radiofemoral delay; coarctation shows upper extremity hypertension with lower extremity hypotension and a radiofemoral delay.

differential_diagnoses.name: Takayasu arteritis
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Systemic inflammation (elevated ESR/CRP), involvement of multiple aortic branches, and typical age <40 years; coarctation is a congenital focal narrowing without systemic inflammation.

differential_diagnoses.name: Hypoplastic left heart syndrome
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Echocardiography shows a hypoplastic left ventricle and ascending aorta; coarctation shows a normal-sized left ventricle with a discrete aortic narrowing.

key_features: Upper extremity hypertension with lower extremity hypotension (blood pressure gradient ≥20 mmHg between arms and legs).
Radiofemoral delay and diminished or absent femoral pulses.
Systolic murmur over the left infrascapular area (continuous or ejection) and possibly a systolic click from a bicuspid aortic valve.
Chest X-ray: rib notching (in older children/adults) and a '3' sign from post-stenotic aortic dilation.
Echocardiography or MRI/CT angiography demonstrating a discrete narrowing of the descending aorta, often just distal to the left subclavian artery.
pitfalls: Often mistaken for essential hypertension because upper extremity hypertension is the presenting sign; coarctation is differentiated by the blood pressure gradient between arms and legs and radiofemoral delay.

The diagnosis is missed in neonates when heart failure and weak pulses are attributed to sepsis or congenital heart disease without measuring four-limb blood pressures and performing echocardiography.

differential_diagnoses.name: Rubella
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Rubella rash is diffuse, maculopapular, and spreads from face to trunk with postauricular lymphadenopathy; fifth disease has slapped-cheek rash followed by lacy reticular rash on extremities.

differential_diagnoses.name: Measles
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Measles presents with high fever, cough, coryza, conjunctivitis, and Koplik spots before a descending maculopapular rash; fifth disease lacks these prodromal symptoms and has a distinctive lacy rash.

differential_diagnoses.name: Drug eruption
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: History of medication exposure and often eosinophilia; fifth disease is virally mediated with positive parvovirus B19 IgM and no drug history.

differential_diagnoses.name: Roseola infantum
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Roseola presents with high fever for 3-5 days followed by a rash that appears as fever defervesces; fifth disease rash appears without a preceding high fever and has a lacy pattern.

key_features: Prodromal mild fever and malaise followed by a 'slapped-cheek' facial rash and a lacy, reticular rash on the trunk and extremities.
Rash may wax and wane and is often exacerbated by heat, sunlight, or bathing.
Positive parvovirus B19 IgM antibody or viral DNA detection in serum.
In children, the illness is typically mild and self-limited; in adults, arthralgia/arthritis may predominate.
Infection during pregnancy can cause fetal anemia, hydrops fetalis, or fetal loss.
pitfalls: Often mistaken for rubella or measles because of the facial rash; fifth disease is differentiated by the lacy reticular rash on extremities and absence of Koplik spots or postauricular lymphadenopathy.
The diagnosis is missed when the rash is attributed to an allergic drug reaction, especially if the patient recently started a new medication, without considering parvovirus B19 serology.

differential_diagnoses.name: Immune thrombocytopenia (ITP)
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Isolated thrombocytopenia with normal platelet function studies; Glanzmann thrombasthenia has normal platelet count but defective aggregation.

differential_diagnoses.name: Bernard-Soulier syndrome
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Giant platelets and thrombocytopenia with defective ristocetin-induced aggregation; Glanzmann has normal platelet count and normal ristocetin aggregation but absent aggregation with ADP, collagen, and epinephrine.

differential_diagnoses.name: von Willebrand disease
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Prolonged bleeding time with abnormal ristocetin cofactor activity and low von Willebrand factor antigen; Glanzmann has normal vWF studies and normal ristocetin aggregation.

differential_diagnoses.name: Platelet storage pool disorder
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Abnormal platelet aggregation with ADP and epinephrine but normal response to arachidonic acid; Glanzmann lacks aggregation with all agonists except ristocetin.

key_features: Mucocutaneous bleeding (epistaxis, gingival bleeding, menorrhagia, petechiae) from early childhood.
Normal platelet count and morphology on peripheral smear.
Platelet aggregation studies: absent or markedly reduced aggregation in response to ADP, collagen, epinephrine, and arachidonic acid, with normal agglutination to ristocetin.
Flow cytometry showing absent or markedly reduced platelet glycoprotein IIb/IIIa (integrin αIIbβ3) and normal glycoprotein Ib/IX/V.
Autosomal recessive inheritance; genetic testing reveals mutations in ITGA2B or ITGB3.
pitfalls: Often mistaken for immune thrombocytopenia because of mucocutaneous bleeding, but platelet count is normal in Glanzmann and aggregation studies are diagnostic.

The diagnosis is missed when bleeding is attributed to a coagulation factor deficiency and platelet function tests are not performed, delaying appropriate management (e.g., platelet transfusions, antifibrinolytics).

differential_diagnoses.name: Osteosarcoma
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Osteosarcoma shows osteoid matrix production and malignant osteoid on histology; giant cell tumor lacks osteoid and has mononuclear neoplastic cells with numerous osteoclast-like giant cells.

differential_diagnoses.name: Chondroblastoma
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Chondroblastoma occurs in the epiphysis of long bones in skeletally immature patients and shows chondroid matrix and 'chicken-wire' calcification; giant cell tumor occurs in the epiphysis of skeletally mature adults without chondroid matrix.

differential_diagnoses.name: Aneurysmal bone cyst
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Aneurysmal bone cyst shows blood-filled cystic spaces on imaging and histology; giant cell tumor is solid and lacks these cystic spaces.

differential_diagnoses.name: Brown tumor of hyperparathyroidism
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Brown tumor is associated with elevated serum calcium and PTH; giant cell tumor has normal calcium and PTH levels.

differential_diagnoses.name: Metastatic carcinoma
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Metastasis often occurs in older patients with a known primary and shows epithelial markers on immunohistochemistry; giant cell tumor has mononuclear cells that are negative for epithelial markers.

key_features: Epiphyseal lytic lesion in a long bone (often distal femur or proximal tibia) in a skeletally mature young adult (20-40 years).
Imaging: well-defined, eccentric, lytic lesion without a sclerotic rim, often extending to the subarticular bone.
Histology: mononuclear neoplastic cells with numerous multinucleated osteoclast-like giant cells uniformly distributed.
Local aggressiveness with potential for recurrence and rare metastasis (usually to lungs).
Association with H3-3A (H3F3A) mutations in the neoplastic mononuclear cells.
pitfalls: Often mistaken for osteosarcoma because both are lytic bone lesions in young adults; giant cell tumor is distinguished by its epiphyseal location, lack of osteoid matrix, and characteristic histology.
The diagnosis is missed when a lytic lesion is attributed to a brown tumor without checking calcium and PTH levels, especially in patients with hyperparathyroidism.

differential_diagnoses.name: Parkinson disease
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Parkinson disease shows asymmetric onset, rest tremor, and sustained levodopa response; MSA typically has symmetric parkinsonism, poor levodopa response, and early autonomic failure.

differential_diagnoses.name: Dementia with Lewy bodies
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: DLB presents with early cognitive fluctuations, visual hallucinations, and REM sleep behavior disorder; MSA has prominent autonomic failure and cerebellar/pyramidal signs without early dementia.

differential_diagnoses.name: Progressive supranuclear palsy
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: PSP shows vertical supranuclear gaze palsy and early falls; MSA features autonomic failure and cerebellar ataxia without supranuclear gaze palsy.

differential_diagnoses.name: Pure autonomic failure
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: PAF has isolated autonomic failure without parkinsonism, cerebellar ataxia, or pyramidal signs; MSA includes these motor features.

key_features: Autonomic failure (orthostatic hypotension, urinary incontinence, erectile dysfunction) plus parkinsonism and/or cerebellar ataxia.
Poor or absent response to levodopa in the parkinsonian subtype (MSA-P).
Cerebellar signs (ataxia, dysarthria, nystagmus) in the cerebellar subtype (MSA-C).
MRI findings: 'hot cross bun' sign in the pons (MSA-C) and putaminal atrophy with slit-like hyperintensity (MSA-P).
Pathology: alpha-synuclein-positive glial cytoplasmic inclusions in oligodendrocytes.
pitfalls: Often mistaken for Parkinson disease because of parkinsonism; MSA is differentiated by early autonomic failure, symmetric signs, and poor levodopa response.
The diagnosis is missed when autonomic symptoms are attributed to aging or medication side effects, delaying recognition of MSA.

differential_diagnoses.name: Malrotation with volvulus
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Upper GI series shows a corkscrew appearance of the duodenum and a misplaced cecum; duodenal atresia shows a dilated proximal duodenum with a distal cutoff ('double bubble') and no distal gas.

differential_diagnoses.name: Jejunoileal atresia
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Abdominal X-ray shows multiple dilated bowel loops with air-fluid levels and distal gas; duodenal atresia shows the 'double bubble' sign with no distal gas.

differential_diagnoses.name: Annular pancreas
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Annular pancreas may cause duodenal obstruction but imaging shows pancreatic tissue encircling the duodenum; duodenal atresia is a congenital absence of the lumen.

differential_diagnoses.name: Duodenal web
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Duodenal web may cause partial obstruction with a 'windsock' deformity on contrast study; duodenal atresia causes complete obstruction with no distal gas.

key_features: Bilious vomiting in a neonate within the first day of life.
Abdominal X-ray showing the 'double bubble' sign (dilated stomach and proximal duodenum) with no distal bowel gas.
Association with Down syndrome (trisomy 21) in about 30% of cases.
Prenatal ultrasound may show polyhydramnios and a double bubble.
Failure to pass meconium in the first 24 hours.
pitfalls: Often mistaken for malrotation with volvulus because both cause bilious vomiting; duodenal atresia is differentiated by the double bubble sign and absence of distal gas on X-ray.
The diagnosis is missed when the double bubble is attributed to a normal stomach bubble and no further imaging is obtained, especially in a stable-appearing neonate.

differential_diagnoses.name: Reactive thrombocytosis
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Reactive thrombocytosis is associated with an elevated CRP/ESR and a secondary cause (infection, inflammation, iron deficiency); essential thrombocythemia lacks these and shows clonal markers (JAK2, CALR, MPL mutations).

differential_diagnoses.name: Polycythemia vera
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Polycythemia vera shows elevated hemoglobin/hematocrit and often low erythropoietin; essential thrombocythemia has normal hemoglobin and hematocrit.

differential_diagnoses.name: Primary myelofibrosis
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Primary myelofibrosis shows leukoerythroblastosis, teardrop cells, and bone marrow fibrosis; essential thrombocythemia lacks these and has megakaryocytic hyperplasia without fibrosis.

differential_diagnoses.name: Chronic myeloid leukemia
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: CML is characterized by the BCR-ABL1 fusion gene and marked leukocytosis with left shift; essential thrombocythemia lacks BCR-ABL1 and has isolated thrombocytosis.

key_features: Sustained thrombocytosis (platelet count ≥450 × 10^9/L) with megakaryocytic hyperplasia on bone marrow biopsy.
Presence of JAK2 V617F (about 50%), CALR (about 25%), or MPL (about 5%) mutations.
Absence of the BCR-ABL1 fusion gene and no evidence of reactive thrombocytosis.
Thrombotic or hemorrhagic complications (e.g., erythromelalgia, stroke, myocardial infarction, bleeding).
Splenomegaly may be present but is usually mild.
pitfalls: Often mistaken for reactive thrombocytosis because both show elevated platelets; essential thrombocythemia is differentiated by clonal mutation testing and absence of an inflammatory or iron-deficiency cause.
The diagnosis is missed when thrombocytosis is attributed to iron deficiency without checking for clonal markers, especially in older patients with persistent thrombocytosis.

differential_diagnoses.name: Nephrolithiasis (uncomplicated)
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Uncomplicated nephrolithiasis shows stones without medullary cysts; MSK shows multiple small cysts in the renal medulla on imaging (e.g., 'paintbrush' appearance on IV urography).

differential_diagnoses.name: Polycystic kidney disease
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: ADPKD shows enlarged kidneys with numerous cysts throughout the cortex and medulla; MSK has normal-sized kidneys with cysts confined to the medullary pyramids.

differential_diagnoses.name: Renal tubular acidosis (distal)
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Distal RTA may cause nephrocalcinosis but lacks the cystic medullary changes of MSK; MSK can cause distal RTA, but the cystic changes are diagnostic.

differential_diagnoses.name: Papillary necrosis
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Papillary necrosis shows sloughed papillae and clubbed calyces on imaging; MSK shows cystic dilation of collecting ducts without papillary sloughing.

key_features: Recurrent calcium nephrolithiasis and nephrocalcinosis in a young adult.
Imaging: medullary cysts (collecting duct dilation) seen as striated or 'paintbrush' appearance on IV urography or as multiple small cysts on CT urography.
Normal kidney size and function in most cases, though some progress to chronic kidney disease.
Associated with hypercalciuria, hypocitraturia, and distal renal tubular acidosis.
Often asymptomatic and discovered incidentally on imaging.
pitfalls: Often mistaken for simple nephrolithiasis because both cause stones; MSK is differentiated by the characteristic medullary cysts on imaging.
The diagnosis is missed when recurrent stones are attributed to dietary factors without imaging that reveals the medullary cystic changes.

differential_diagnoses.name: Vaginismus (older term)
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Vaginismus is now subsumed under GPPPD; the distinguishing feature is that GPPPD includes both pain and penetration difficulties, whereas vaginismus historically referred only to involuntary muscle spasm.

differential_diagnoses.name: Dyspareunia due to organic causes (e.g., endometriosis)
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Endometriosis shows pelvic pain with menses, dyschezia, and laparoscopic evidence of endometrial implants; GPPPD has no organic pathology and pain is associated with penetration.

differential_diagnoses.name: Vulvodynia
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Vulvodynia is vulvar pain without penetration difficulty; GPPPD includes fear or avoidance of penetration and pelvic floor muscle tension.

differential_diagnoses.name: Sexual desire/arousal disorder
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Sexual desire/arousal disorder involves low desire or arousal without pain; GPPPD is characterized by pain and penetration difficulties.

key_features: Persistent or recurrent difficulties with vaginal penetration during intercourse, gynecologic exams, or tampon use.
Marked genito-pelvic pain or fear/anxiety about pain during penetration.
Tensing of the pelvic floor muscles during attempted penetration.
Symptoms cause clinically significant distress or impairment and are not better explained by another mental disorder or medical condition.
Diagnosis is clinical, based on history and examination; organic causes should be excluded.
pitfalls: Often mistaken for vulvodynia because both involve genital pain; GPPPD is differentiated by the prominent fear and avoidance of penetration and pelvic floor muscle tension.
The diagnosis is missed when symptoms are attributed to a physical cause (e.g., infection) without addressing the psychological and muscular components.

differential_diagnoses.name: Chronic hepatitis C
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Positive HCV RNA and anti-HCV antibodies; chronic hepatitis B has positive HBsAg and HBV DNA.

differential_diagnoses.name: Autoimmune hepatitis
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Positive ANA/ASMA, elevated IgG, and interface hepatitis on biopsy; chronic hepatitis B has positive HBsAg and lacks these autoantibodies.

differential_diagnoses.name: Wilson disease
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Low ceruloplasmin, elevated urinary copper, and Kayser-Fleischer rings; chronic hepatitis B has positive HBV serologies and normal copper studies.

differential_diagnoses.name: Nonalcoholic steatohepatitis
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Histology shows steatosis and ballooning degeneration without significant inflammation; chronic hepatitis B shows positive HBsAg and necroinflammation.

key_features: Positive HBsAg for >6 months, often with positive HBeAg and high HBV DNA levels.
Elevated aminotransferases (ALT/AST) and necroinflammation on liver biopsy.
Risk of progression to cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma.
May be asymptomatic or present with fatigue, jaundice, or signs of chronic liver disease.
Serology may show IgM anti-HBc in flares, indicating active viral replication.
pitfalls: Often mistaken for autoimmune hepatitis because both cause elevated aminotransferases and interface hepatitis; chronic hepatitis B is differentiated by positive HBsAg and HBV DNA.
The diagnosis is missed when HBsAg is not tested in patients with elevated liver enzymes, especially in those from endemic areas.

differential_diagnoses.name: Acute pancreatitis
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Elevated serum lipase (>3 times upper limit) and characteristic epigastric pain radiating to the back; acute mesenteric ischemia has pain out of proportion to exam and often normal lipase.

differential_diagnoses.name: Small bowel obstruction
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Abdominal X-ray/CT shows dilated bowel loops with air-fluid levels and a transition point; acute mesenteric ischemia may show bowel wall thickening, pneumatosis, or portal venous gas.

differential_diagnoses.name: Perforated viscus
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Free air on upright chest X-ray or CT; acute mesenteric ischemia may cause perforation but typically presents with pain out of proportion and no free air initially.

differential_diagnoses.name: Renal colic
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: Flank pain with hematuria and hydronephrosis on CT; acute mesenteric ischemia has abdominal pain out of proportion and often lactic acidosis.

key_features: Severe abdominal pain out of proportion to physical findings, often in a patient with risk factors (atrial fibrillation, atherosclerosis, recent myocardial infarction).
Elevated lactate and metabolic acidosis; leukocytosis.
CT angiography showing arterial or venous occlusion, bowel wall thickening, pneumatosis intestinalis, or portal venous gas.
Early findings may be subtle; delayed diagnosis leads to bowel infarction and high mortality.
May present with 'intestinal angina' (postprandial pain) in chronic forms, but acute onset is sudden and severe.
pitfalls: Often mistaken for acute pancreatitis because both cause severe epigastric pain; acute mesenteric ischemia is differentiated by pain out of proportion to exam, elevated lactate, and CT angiography findings.
The diagnosis is missed when pain is attributed to gastroenteritis or ileus and CT angiography is not performed, especially in elderly patients with atrial fibrillation.

differential_diagnoses.name: COPD
differential_diagnoses.distinguishing_feature: COPD shows fixed airflow obstruction with reduced FEV1/FVC ratio that does not fully reverse with bronchodilators; asthma shows reversible obstruction (≥12% and 200 mL improvement in FEV1).

differential_diagnoses.name: Vocal cord dysfunction
